name: vscode-nexterminal
description: Full SSH + serial + port-forwarding client inside VS Code — no 300MB Remote-SSH agent on the box. Built for network and infra engineers: SSH, serial consoles, jump-host chains, SFTP, tunnels, expect/send macros with prompted variables, and a JS scripting engine, all in one sidebar. Bulk-import devices from CSV or a plain host list, save root-owned files over SFTP with sudo, import from MobaXterm/SecureCRT, NetBox inventory sync with auth profiles and device templates, IPv6/IPv4 dual-address connect-fallback, 2FA, legacy KEX for old Cisco gear.

nexus.logging.maxFileSizeMb.markdownDescription: Maximum size of each Nexus log file in MB before rotation.

nexus.logging.maxRotatedFiles.markdownDescription: How many rotated log files Nexus keeps per log stream.

nexus.logging.sessionTranscripts.markdownDescription: Log session transcripts for SSH and serial connections by default. Can be overridden per profile.

nexus.logging.sessionLogDirectory.markdownDescription: Directory for session transcript logs. Leave empty to use the default extension storage location.

nexus.logging.terminalOutputTrace.markdownDescription:
Troubleshooting only. Write every chunk of terminal output to the diagnostic log as it arrives.

Leave this off unless support asks for it. It writes to disk once for every chunk a session receives, which adds latency to terminal output, and it records session data verbatim — including anything typed or echoed on screen, such as passwords and keys — as plaintext in the extension's log folder. Session transcripts (`#nexus.logging.sessionTranscripts#`) are the supported way to keep a record of a session.

nexus.tunnel.defaultConnectionMode.markdownDescription: Default SSH connection mode for tunnels.
enumDescriptions: Each TCP client gets its own SSH connection (use only when connection isolation is critical)
All clients share a single SSH connection (recommended — works with 2FA, lower resource usage)

nexus.tunnel.defaultBindAddress.markdownDescription: Default bind address for reverse tunnels. Use `127.0.0.1` for local-only or `0.0.0.0` for all interfaces (requires `GatewayPorts` on the SSH server).

nexus.ssh.multiplexing.enabled.markdownDescription: Share a single SSH connection per server across terminals, tunnels (shared mode), and SFTP. Reduces overhead and avoids multiple auth prompts. Requires window reload to take effect.

nexus.ssh.multiplexing.idleTimeout.markdownDescription: Seconds to keep an idle multiplexed connection alive after all channels close (`0` = keep alive until window closes, max `3600`). Requires window reload.

nexus.ssh.trustNewHosts.markdownDescription: Automatically trust SSH host keys on first connection (Trust-On-First-Use). When enabled, you will only be prompted if a host's key **changes** from what was previously stored — which may indicate a man-in-the-middle attack. Disable to be prompted for every new host.

nexus.terminal.openLocation.markdownDescription: Where to open SSH and serial terminals.

nexus.ui.showTreeDescriptions.markdownDescription: Show connection details (e.g. `user@host`) next to device names in the Connectivity Hub tree.

nexus.terminal.keyboardPassthrough.markdownDescription: Pass Ctrl+ key combinations through to the terminal instead of VS Code when the terminal is focused. Enables full use of terminal apps like nano, vim, and htop.

nexus.terminal.passthroughKeys.markdownDescription: Which Ctrl+ key combinations to pass through when `#nexus.terminal.keyboardPassthrough#` is enabled. Each entry is a letter (e.g. `b` for Ctrl+B).

nexus.terminal.macros.autoTrigger.markdownDescription: Enable auto-trigger for macros that have a `triggerPattern`. When terminal output matches the pattern, the macro text is sent automatically.

nexus.terminal.highlighting.enabled.markdownDescription: Enable regex-based pattern highlighting in SSH, serial, and Local Shell terminal output. Matches are coloured inline using ANSI SGR codes while respecting existing terminal colours.

default.label: Critical / fatal errors
default.description: CRITICAL, FATAL, PANIC, EMERG(ENCY) — highest-severity log keywords, bold bright red.

default.label: Errors
default.description: ERR / ERROR — general error keyword, bold red.

default.label: Failures / aborts
default.description: FAIL(ED/URE), ABORT(ED) — operation failed or was aborted, bold red.

default.label: Warnings
default.description: WARN / WARNING — cautionary log keyword, bold yellow.

default.label: Notices
default.description: NOTICE — informational-but-notable log keyword, cyan.

default.label: Info
default.description: INFO — routine informational log keyword, cyan.

default.label: Debug / trace
default.description: DEBUG, TRACE — low-priority diagnostic keywords, dimmed grey.

default.label: Success keywords
default.description: OK, PASS(ED), SUCCESS(FUL), DONE, LOADED, STARTED, MOUNTED — positive outcome keywords, bold green.

default.label: Denied / rejected
default.description: DENIED, REJECT(ED), REFUSED, FORBIDDEN, BLOCKED — access/action refused, red.

default.label: Accepted / granted
default.description: ACCEPTED, ALLOWED, GRANTED, AUTHENTICATED — access/action allowed, green.

default.label: Timeout / unreachable
default.description: TIMEOUT, TIMED OUT, UNREACHABLE, NO ROUTE, RESET, RETRANSMIT, DUPLICATE — network/connectivity failure keywords, red.

default.label: Down / inactive (case-sensitive)
default.description: DOWN, INACTIVE, DISABLED, OFFLINE, DEAD — case-sensitive so lowercase prose words aren't matched, red.

default.label: Up / active (case-sensitive)
default.description: UP, ACTIVE, ENABLED, RUNNING, ESTABLISHED, CONNECTED, ONLINE, ALIVE, REACHABLE — case-sensitive so lowercase prose words aren't matched, green.

default.label: Pending / waiting
default.description: PENDING, WAITING, LISTENING, STARTING, RELOADING, STOPPING — transitional state keywords, yellow.

default.label: Deprecated
default.description: DEPRECATED, OBSOLETE — flags outdated commands/features, underlined yellow.

default.label: MAC addresses
default.description: Colon- or hyphen-separated MAC addresses (e.g. aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff), magenta.

default.label: IPv4 addresses
default.description: IPv4 addresses, optionally with a /prefix (e.g. 10.0.0.1/24), magenta.

default.label: IPv6 addresses
default.description: IPv6 addresses, full and compressed (including trailing-compressed forms like fe80:: or 2001:db8::), except the bare all-zeros "::" — a lone :: in terminal output is overwhelmingly a C++/Ruby scope operator. Disabled by default — this is one of the two most expensive built-in patterns, since it has to be tried at nearly every character. Enable it from the Highlighting Rules editor if you want it.

default.label: UUIDs
default.description: Standard 8-4-4-4-12 hex UUIDs. Disabled by default — this is one of the two most expensive built-in patterns, since it has to be tried at nearly every character. Enable it from the Highlighting Rules editor if you want it.

default.label: URLs
default.description: http(s):// links, underlined blue.

default.label: Interface error counters
default.description: Network-interface error counter labels (errors, dropped, CRC, collisions, overruns, …), red.

default.label: Exit-code / signal keywords
default.description: exit-code, core-dump, signal, timeout, watchdog — process-death diagnostic keywords, red.

pattern.description: Regular expression pattern to match in terminal output.

color.description: Named colour (red, green, brightCyan, …) or raw SGR code number (e.g. "31").

bold.description: Apply bold style to matched text.

underline.description: Apply underline style to matched text.

label.description: Short display name shown in the Highlighting Rules editor.

description.description: What the rule matches / notes, shown in the Highlighting Rules editor.

enabled.description: Set to false to keep the rule but stop applying it.

nexus.terminal.highlighting.rules.markdownDescription:
Highlighting rules applied to SSH, serial, and Local Shell terminal output. Each rule specifies a regex `pattern`, a `color` (named or SGR code), optional `flags`, and optional `bold`/`underline` styles. A rule can also carry an optional `label` and `description` for its own entry in the Highlighting Rules editor, and an optional `enabled` flag (omitted/`true` means enabled) to keep a rule saved without applying it. Text already coloured by the terminal program is never re-highlighted.

The IPv6 and UUID rules ship **disabled** by default: those two patterns cost more than every other rule combined, because they have to be tried at nearly every character of every line. Switch either one on with its per-rule enable checkbox in the Highlighting Rules editor — no need to retype the regex.

nexus.sftp.cacheTtlSeconds.markdownDescription: How long SFTP directory listings are cached (in seconds). Set to `0` to disable caching entirely (every tree expansion fetches fresh data).

nexus.sftp.maxCacheEntries.markdownDescription: Maximum number of directory listings kept in the SFTP cache. Oldest entries are evicted when this limit is exceeded.

nexus.sftp.autoRefreshInterval.markdownDescription: Polling interval for the SFTP File Explorer (in seconds). Used when `remoteWatchMode` is `polling`, and as a safety-net refresh cadence in `auto` mode unless recursive `inotifywait` support is available. Set to `0` to disable polling. Only active when the view is visible and a server is connected.

nexus.sftp.remoteWatchMode.markdownDescription: How the File Explorer detects remote filesystem changes. `auto` prefers recursive `inotifywait` watching when available and otherwise keeps polling enabled as the safety net. `polling` disables remote watch probes and uses only the interval set by `autoRefreshInterval`.

nexus.sftp.maxOpenFileSizeMB.markdownDescription: Maximum size (in MB) of a single file Nexus will hold in memory. Applies to opening a remote file in the editor, and to transferring a file whose reported size is `0` (pseudo-files and appliances that mis-report size have to be read to the end to find out how big they are). Ordinary uploads and downloads stream and are not limited by this.

nexus.ssh.connectionTimeout.markdownDescription: SSH connection timeout in seconds. Increase for slow or high-latency networks.

nexus.ssh.keepaliveInterval.markdownDescription: Interval in seconds between SSH keepalive packets. Set to `0` to disable keepalives.

nexus.ssh.keepaliveCountMax.markdownDescription: Number of missed keepalive responses before the connection is considered dead.

nexus.ssh.terminalType.markdownDescription: Terminal type (`$TERM`) reported to the remote server.
enumDescriptions: Minimal terminal with no special capabilities

nexus.ssh.proxyTimeout.markdownDescription: Timeout in seconds for proxy handshake (SOCKS5 or HTTP CONNECT) when connecting through a proxy.

nexus.sftp.operationTimeout.markdownDescription: Timeout in seconds for SFTP directory and metadata operations (listing, stat, realpath, rename, mkdir, delete). Prevents the file explorer from freezing when the shared SSH connection is congested.

nexus.sftp.commandTimeout.markdownDescription: Timeout in seconds for remote SFTP commands (e.g. server-side copy), file transfers, and editor file open/save streams. Upload/download treat this as an inactivity timeout, so long transfers can continue while progress is still flowing.

nexus.sftp.deleteDepthLimit.markdownDescription: ⚠ **Safety limit** — Maximum directory nesting depth for recursive delete operations.

nexus.sftp.deleteOperationLimit.markdownDescription: ⚠ **Safety limit** — Maximum number of files and directories that can be deleted in a single recursive delete.

nexus.sftp.sudo.enabled.description: Offer to save remote files with sudo when the SSH user lacks write permission.

nexus.sftp.sudo.rememberPasswordForSessi.description: Keep the sudo password in memory until that server disconnects or the window closes, rather than clearing it after each save. Never written to disk or to VS Code's secret storage. Turning this off does not guarantee a prompt on every save: the remote host's own sudo credential timestamp (~5 minutes) can skip it regardless, and a short grace window (30 seconds) after you enter a password also covers an immediately-following elevated save on the same server either way.

nexus.tunnel.socks5HandshakeTimeout.markdownDescription: Timeout in seconds for the SOCKS5 proxy handshake on dynamic tunnels.

nexus.terminal.macros.defaultCooldown.markdownDescription: Default cooldown in seconds between auto-trigger firings on the same terminal. Individual macros can override this with `triggerCooldown`.

nexus.terminal.macros.bufferLength.markdownDescription: Maximum number of characters kept in the auto-trigger prompt buffer per terminal. Larger values allow matching against more terminal output.

nexus.serial.rpcTimeout.markdownDescription: Timeout in seconds for commands sent to the serial port sidecar process.

nexus.scripts.path.markdownDescription: Directory where Nexus scripts live. Relative paths are resolved against the workspace root. When no workspace is open, scripts are stored in the extension's global storage regardless of this setting. An absolute path is used as-is in both cases. Use the Nexus Settings page (Connectivity Hub → Settings) for a folder picker.

nexus.scripts.defaultTimeoutSeconds.markdownDescription: Default per-wait timeout in seconds, used by `waitFor` / `expect` / `waitAny` when a script doesn't pass its own `timeout`. Override per script via the `@default-timeout` JSDoc tag, or per call via the `timeout` option.

enumDescriptions: Suspend all auto-trigger macros on the script's bound session for the duration of the run (default).
Keep all macros enabled. Use only if you understand the risk of macros firing alongside script-driven input.
nexus.scripts.macroPolicy.markdownDescription: How the script runtime treats macro auto-triggers on the bound session while a script is running.

nexus.scripts.maxRuntimeSeconds.markdownDescription: Maximum total runtime for a script in seconds. 0 disables the cap. The script is stopped with reason `max-runtime-exceeded` if it exceeds this. Values are capped at 2147483 seconds, the largest safe VS Code/Node timer delay.

nexus.scripts.maxRuntimeMs.markdownDescription: Legacy maximum total runtime for a script in milliseconds. Prefer `nexus.scripts.maxRuntimeSeconds`. 0 disables the cap.

nexus.settingsGuard.enabled.markdownDescription: Automatically restore `terminal.integrated.commandsToSkipShell` entries when an external program (e.g. a corporate DLP/endpoint agent) strips them from `settings.json`. Restores are rate-limited and every restore shows an Undo notification. Forensic logging (see *Nexus: Show Settings Guard Report*) stays active even when this is disabled.

nexus.localServers.defaultMaxAutoRestart.markdownDescription: Default maximum number of automatic restarts per local server when `autoRestart` is enabled and no explicit `maxAutoRestarts` is set on the profile. 0 disables auto-restart globally. Auto-restart uses exponential backoff and stops counting attempts after 10 seconds of stable runtime.

nexus.localServers.stableRuntimeMs.markdownDescription: Milliseconds of continuous runtime after which a local server is considered 'stable' and its auto-restart attempt counter is reset. Must be long enough to distinguish a real crash from a graceful exit triggered just after startup.

nexus.localServers.initialBackoffMs.markdownDescription: Initial exponential-backoff delay in milliseconds before the first auto-restart. Each subsequent attempt doubles this value up to `nexus.localServers.maxBackoffMs`.

nexus.localServers.maxBackoffMs.markdownDescription: Maximum backoff delay in milliseconds between auto-restart attempts (exponential backoff ceiling).

nexus.localServers.restrictToWorkspaceRo.markdownDescription: Refuse to start a local server whose working directory resolves outside the currently-open workspace roots when a workspace is open. Disabling this allows any absolute path, including system directories, as cwd — enable only if you trust every profile in storage.

nexus.networkServers.tftp.root.markdownDescription: **TFTP — Network.** Directory served by the embedded TFTP service. Leave empty to use `~/Nexus/tftp-root`, which is created on first start (falling back to the system temp directory if it cannot be created). **Every file beneath this directory is readable by any host that can reach the bound port** — point it at a staging directory, not at a source tree or a home directory.

nexus.networkServers.tftp.interface.markdownDescription: **TFTP — Network.** Local IPv4 address to bind the TFTP socket to, i.e. which network interface serves TFTP. Leave empty for `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces). On a multi-homed machine, set this to the lab-facing NIC (e.g. `192.168.2.1`) so the service is not also reachable over the corporate LAN or VPN. This address is also what `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.autoLinkTftp#` advertises to DHCP clients, so binding all interfaces leaves the DHCP boot options unset. *Edit Settings on the TFTP service offers this machine's addresses as a list.*

nexus.networkServers.tftp.port.markdownDescription: **TFTP — Network.** UDP port for the embedded TFTP service. The IANA port 69 is privileged: if binding it is denied (no root/Administrator), the service automatically falls back to **1069** and logs a warning instead of failing. Clients must then be pointed at the fallback port — the port actually in use is shown next to the service.

nexus.networkServers.tftp.allowWrite.markdownDescription: **TFTP — Access.** Accept TFTP write requests (`WRQ`), letting remote clients upload files into `#nexus.networkServers.tftp.root#`. TFTP has no authentication whatsoever, so anything that can reach the port can overwrite files. Leave disabled unless a device genuinely needs to push configs or crash dumps back.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.interface.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Network.** Local IPv4 address to bind the DHCP socket to, i.e. which network interface serves DHCP. Leave empty for `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces) — on a multi-homed machine this is what stops a lab DHCP server from answering DISCOVERs arriving on the corporate LAN. The service always uses the IANA port 67; if binding it is denied (no root/Administrator), it automatically falls back to **1067** and logs a warning, which normal DHCP clients will not reach. *Edit Settings on the DHCP service offers this machine's addresses as a list.*

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.rangeStart.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Address Pool.** First address of the dynamic pool. Leave empty for `192.168.2.10`. Must not be higher than `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.rangeEnd#`; addresses reserved in `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.static#` are handed out regardless of this range.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.rangeEnd.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Address Pool.** Last address of the dynamic pool. Leave empty for `192.168.2.199`. The pool size this implies drives the utilization figure shown beside the running service.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.subnet.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Address Pool.** Subnet mask handed to clients (option 1). Leave empty for `255.255.255.0`. Its set bits must be contiguous (`255.255.254.0` is a mask, `255.0.255.0` is not); together with `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.gateway#` it also derives `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.broadcast#` when that is left empty.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.gateway.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Address Pool.** Default gateway handed to clients (option 3). Leave empty for `192.168.2.1`.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.dns.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Address Pool.** DNS servers handed to clients (option 6), in preference order. Leave empty for `8.8.8.8` and `8.8.4.4`.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.leaseTimeSec.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Address Pool.** Lease duration in seconds (option 51). Clamped to 60 seconds minimum — shorter leases make clients renew faster than the server can meaningfully track — and 7 days maximum.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.serverId.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Address Pool.** Server identifier advertised to clients (option 54). Leave empty for `192.168.2.1`. This should be the address clients see this machine on, otherwise renewals are sent to the wrong host. It is also the value carried in the BOOTP `siaddr` header field, which devices that ignore option 66 boot from.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.broadcast.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Address Pool.** Broadcast address handed to clients (option 28). Leave empty to derive it from `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.gateway#` and `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.subnet#`.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.bootFileName.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Boot / ZTP. Option 67** (bootfile-name) — the file a PXE or ZTP client fetches from the boot server once it has an address, for example `ios-image.bin`, `pxelinux.0` or `ztp.py`. The boot server itself is `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.nextServer#`. Leave empty to send no bootfile, in which case a device gets an address and nothing to boot from.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.nextServer.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Boot / ZTP. Option 66** (tftp-server-name) — the boot server clients fetch `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.bootFileName#` from, as a dotted-quad address (e.g. `192.168.2.1`) or a hostname. Leave empty and `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.autoLinkTftp#` fills it in from the embedded TFTP service's own interface. Note that the BOOTP `siaddr` header field is **not** configurable — it always carries `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.serverId#` — so devices that read `siaddr` instead of option 66 follow that address.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.tftpServerAddr.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Boot / ZTP. Option 150** (Cisco TFTP server address list) — one or more IPv4 addresses, in preference order. Cisco IP phones and IOS ZTP request option 150 rather than `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.nextServer#` (option 66); hardware from other vendors generally ignores it, so setting both is normal. Leave empty and `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.autoLinkTftp#` fills in the embedded TFTP service's own interface.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.autoLinkTftp.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Boot / ZTP.** Point DHCP clients at this machine's own TFTP service. When `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.nextServer#` and `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.tftpServerAddresses#` are both empty, options 66 and 150 are filled in from `#nexus.networkServers.tftp.interface#` so ZTP works without typing the same address twice. Setting either one by hand turns the link off for both — quietly advertising a second, different boot server under the other option number is how a device boots from the wrong host. If the TFTP service is bound to `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces) there is no single address to advertise, and both options are left unset rather than guessed.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.vendorClassId.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Boot / ZTP. Option 60** (vendor class identifier) to match on. When set, the boot options (66, 67, 150 and 43) are served **only** to clients whose DISCOVER carries this exact identifier — everyone else still gets an address from the pool, just no boot information. Aruba, FortiGate and Huawei gear all key their provisioning off option 60. The match is case-insensitive but otherwise exact, so `Cisco` will not match `Cisco Systems, Inc.`; the value each client actually sends is logged (`vendor-class="…"`) in the *Nexus Network Servers* channel at debug level. Leave empty to serve the boot options to every client.

subOption.description: Sub-option code (1-254). 0 is PAD and 255 is END, so neither can carry a value.

value.description: Plain text, or a 0x-prefixed hex literal (e.g. 0x0A0B0C) for raw bytes.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.vendorSpecific.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Boot / ZTP. Option 43** (vendor-specific information) as a list of sub-options, TLV-encoded onto the wire as `[code][length][value]` per RFC 2132 §8.4. Each vendor defines its own sub-option layout — Aruba APs read the controller address from sub-option 43/1, Cisco APs from 241, and so on — so the codes come from the vendor's documentation. A `value` starting with `0x` is written as raw bytes (`:` `-` `_` separators are ignored), anything else is written as text. Like the other boot options this is gated by `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.vendorClassId#` when that is set. The whole option is capped at 255 bytes; an entry that cannot be encoded is logged and skipped rather than blocking the service.

nexus.networkServers.dhcp.static.markdownDescription: **DHCP — Reservations.** Static reservations as a **MAC address → IP address** map, for example `{ "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff": "192.168.2.50" }`. Reserved addresses are handed to the matching client regardless of the dynamic pool, so they may sit inside or outside `#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.rangeStart#`…`#nexus.networkServers.dhcp.rangeEnd#`. Entries whose value is not a string are ignored, so one malformed line does not discard the rest of the map.

nexus.networkServers.verboseMode.markdownDescription: **Network Servers — Notifications.** Show a notification for embedded TFTP and DHCP activity: each Start / Stop / Restart, every TFTP transfer that opens, finishes or fails, and every DHCP lease granted or declined. Off by default because a device booting over ZTP fetches one file per notification and a bench full of hardware leases addresses all day. Failed Start / Stop / Restart commands are always reported regardless of this setting, and the *Nexus Network Servers* output channel records everything either way.

untrustedWorkspaces.description: In Restricted Mode, Local Server Start/Restart commands are disabled and no arbitrary binaries are spawned. The embedded Network Servers (TFTP and DHCP) are disabled too: no privileged UDP ports are bound and no directory is served over the network. Viewing, editing, duplicating, renaming, and inspecting stopped profiles still work.

scripts.build: npm run clean && npm run compile && node esbuild.mjs && npm run prepare:local-pty
scripts.build:production: npm run clean && npm run compile && node esbuild.mjs --production && npm run smoke:bundle && npm run prepare:local-pty
scripts.package:vsix: npm run clean && npm run compile && node esbuild.mjs --production && npm run smoke:bundle && npm run prepare:local-pty:required && vsce package
